authoritative_sources.title: Chapter 10: Identifying Hazards
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Accessible Canadian medical-education source; the page does not state a version or update date. Used only for stable disaster-response concepts, with PHAC used for current Canadian preparedness context.

supported_recommendations.statement: For a health emergency, identify the event and participate in the applicable public-health or emergency-management response structure; Canadian pandemic response planning includes federal, provincial and territorial plans rather than a single interchangeable local procedure.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Do not infer that a federal resource replaces provincial, territorial, local, or site-specific emergency procedures.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Provincial and territorial plans are individual; local operational instructions require verification before use in a scenario.

evidence_notes: Canadian-first sources found. The stable educational framework is paired with current PHAC response-planning context.

authoritative_sources.title: Chapter 10: Identifying Hazards
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Accessible Canadian medical-education source without a stated page version or update date; used for stable occupational-history concepts only.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: AFMC is a Canadian medical-education authority providing the MCC-linked stable occupational assessment framework.

supported_recommendations.statement: When a patient may have a work-related health problem, obtain a focused work and exposure history, including work performed, how it is performed, exposure concerns, co-worker exposure, and job satisfaction.

evidence_boundaries.statement: A work history supports assessment of a possible occupational contribution; it does not by itself establish causation.

source_citations.locator: Hazardous occupations; Risk assessment, Step 3: Exposure assessment

evidence_notes: Canadian alternative source used for stable MCC-linked occupational diagnostic history.

authoritative_sources.title: Chapter 10: Identifying Hazards
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Accessible Canadian medical-education source without a stated page version or update date; used for stable occupational-hazard recognition concepts only.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: AFMC is a Canadian medical-education authority providing the MCC-linked occupational-hazard framework.

supported_recommendations.statement: In a possible occupational illness, identify candidate workplace hazards and classify them (biological, chemical, physical, ergonomic, psychosocial, or safety-related) before assessing the exposure-health relationship.

evidence_boundaries.statement: The listed categories organize potential hazards; a category alone does not establish the dose, route, timing, or causation for an individual patient.

source_citations.locator: Risk assessment; Risk assessment, Step 1: Hazard identification

evidence_notes: Stable diagnostic framing; no current disease-specific recommendation asserted.

authoritative_sources.title: Chapter 10: Identifying Hazards
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Accessible Canadian medical-education source without a stated page version or update date; used for stable occupational injury and disease concepts only.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: AFMC is a Canadian medical-education authority providing the MCC-linked definitions and jurisdictional context.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize that an occupational injury or disease may arise in the course of employment, and consider occupational exposures when evaluating commonly work-related conditions such as dermatitis, asthma, musculoskeletal disorders, or work-related mental-health effects.

source_citations.locator: Occupational injuries and diseases; The Mad Hatter

evidence_boundaries.statement: Precise legal definitions and compensation consequences can vary under provincial occupational-health and workers-compensation law.

source_citations.locator: Occupational injuries and diseases; The Mad Hatter

evidence_notes: Stable recognition content; no province-specific legal instruction is asserted.

authoritative_sources.title: Chapter 10: Identifying Hazards
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Accessible Canadian medical-education source without a stated page version or update date; used for stable exposure-assessment concepts only.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: AFMC is a Canadian medical-education authority providing the MCC-linked stable exposure-assessment framework.

supported_recommendations.statement: Assess a suspected occupational exposure by determining the activities, work practices, processes, route, extent, and timing of exposure; include prior work when delayed effects are plausible.

evidence_boundaries.statement: An exposure assessment estimates exposure and informs risk characterization; it does not replace condition-specific diagnostic testing or specialist assessment when indicated.

source_citations.locator: Risk assessment, Step 3: Exposure assessment; Risk assessment, Step 4: Risk characterization

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: For hazards with delayed effects, an occupational history may need to trace exposures back twenty years or more.

evidence_notes: Stable occupational diagnostic framework; no disease-specific management claim included.

authoritative_sources.title: Depression—Clinician Summary
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Current Task Force clinician page. It is used only to establish screening’s evidence benefit-harm framework, not as a general recommendation for a disease outside the page’s stated population.

supported_recommendations.statement: Assess screening using current, condition-specific Canadian guidance that weighs demonstrable benefits against harms; do not assume that screening asymptomatic people is beneficial merely because a condition is important.

source_citations.locator: Basis of recommendation; Considerations for implementation

evidence_boundaries.statement: The cited Task Force recommendation applies to screening asymptomatic adults for depression and should not be extrapolated to a different screening program.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Symptomatic patients require appropriate clinical assessment; that is distinct from routine population screening.

source_citations.locator: Considerations for implementation—Remain aware of signs and clinical clues of depression
Basis of recommendation; Considerations for implementation

evidence_notes: Screening is a policy-sensitive area; the packet deliberately supports only the general evidence-appraisal principle and preserves condition-specific guidance boundaries.

authoritative_sources.title: Chapter 5: Assessing Evidence and Information
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Accessible Canadian medical-education source without a stated page version or update date; used for stable epidemiology and critical-appraisal concepts only.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: AFMC is a Canadian medical-education authority providing the MCC-linked critical-appraisal framework.

supported_recommendations.statement: When appraising an exposure-outcome association, consider bias and confounding: confounding can occur when a third variable is associated with both the exposure and outcome and is not accounted for in analysis.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Association, statistical significance, or a plausible mechanism alone does not establish causation when bias or confounding remains possible.

source_citations.locator: Confounding; Dr. Rao judges the evidence

evidence_notes: Stable conceptual packet. No source-specific clinical recommendation or quantitative causal estimate is asserted.

authoritative_sources.title: Common Definitions on Cultural Safety: Chief Public Health Officer Health Professional Forum
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: PHAC-hosted national Health Professional Forum definitions for contemporary Indigenous cultural safety and humility in health care.

supported_recommendations.statement: In care involving First Nations, Inuit, or Métis patients, use culturally safe and humble practice: engage respectfully, address power imbalances and racism, and recognize that safety is determined by the patient’s experience rather than by clinician intent alone.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Cultural safety is an ongoing, patient-experienced outcome; it is not established merely by completing awareness training or applying a generic cultural stereotype.

source_citations.locator: Continuum of cultural safety and humility; Cultural awareness; Cultural safety

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Engagement with First Nations, Inuit, and Métis must be distinctions-based and reflect each people’s unique interests, priorities, and circumstances.

evidence_notes: Current Canadian PHAC guidance selected. The management claim is limited to culturally safe practice and does not assert a treatment protocol or jurisdiction-specific entitlement.
